screens.title: Other Architectural Evaluation Techniques
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we broaden the toolbox for evaluating architectures. You will learn how organizations use standing review groups, lightweight artifacts like checklists, technical experiments such as simulations and prototypes, and automated static checks to validate design choices. These techniques are not a replacement for a rigorous method; they are complementary. An Architecture Review Board leverages collective experience to catch policy and consistency issues early. Checklists and questionnaires provide a quick compliance baseline for common risks like security and scalability. Simulations let you model performance trade-offs without building the whole system. Prototypes provide concrete proofs of feasibility for risky integrations. Static analysis enforces architectural rules continuously, preventing long-term design drift. Choosing among these methods depends on size, criticality, budget, and the quality attributes you must protect. For example, a small team working on an internal tool might rely on checklists and periodic ARB reviews, while a critical system may add prototypes for high-risk components and static rules in CI. As you proceed, think about which mix reduces risk for your project most efficiently. What single risk would you tackle first with the techniques here?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Selection & Combination
Select and Combine Techniques
A quick decision framework to match technique to risk.
Decision Flow
  1. Identify the highest-risk quality attribute to protect.
  2. Estimate cost and expertise required for each technique.
  3. Choose minimal combination to reduce that risk effectively.
  4. Plan for continuous enforcement where needed.
Example mix
For a high-criticality service: ATAM if available, ARB for governance, prototype for latency, and static analysis in CI for long-term integrity.
Common pitfall
Treating a prototype as production-ready leads to hidden technical debt. Use prototypes for learning, not shipping.
Checklist
  • Is the technique aligned with the primary risk?
  • Is the required effort justified by the potential impact?
  • Will feedback be actionable and timely?

screens.title: Architecture Review Board (ARB)
screens.narratorSegment: An Architecture Review Board is a standing committee of experienced architects and senior technical leaders who review proposed designs and advise teams. The ARB's value is collective experience and organizational consistency: it ensures architectural standards are applied, lessons learned across projects are shared, and potentially risky design decisions are questioned before they propagate. A typical ARB review is structured but less formal than a full ATAM. The presenting architect explains goals, key risks, and major decisions. Reviewers ask probing questions, request clarifications, and may recommend changes or approval. For example, an ARB might flag a proposed direct database access from a presentation component, reminding the team to route through business logic to preserve separation of concerns. A common misconception is that ARBs are gatekeepers who block progress. In healthy practice an ARB is advisory and collaborative: it surfaces constraints and trade-offs, not stop work. To make ARBs effective, define clear scope, keep meetings time-boxed, prepare concise artifacts, and focus on decisions that affect cross-project consistency. Key takeaway: an ARB amplifies organizational wisdom and enforces standards, but it must be structured to enable teams rather than slow them. How would you present a risky decision to an ARB to get constructive guidance?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Architecture Review Board
Definition
Standing committee for design reviews

An ARB reviews proposals, enforces standards, and shares lessons across teams.

How an ARB runs
  • Periodic meetings with concise proposal artifacts.
  • Present decisions, key trade-offs, and risks.
  • Board provides feedback and guidance.
Common mistake
Allowing the ARB to act as a gatekeeper that delays innovation instead of advising teams.
Example & Guidance
Scenario: Presentation layer accessing database
An ARB questions a direct database call from UI code, prompting the architect to show how business rules will be preserved by inserting a service layer.
Pro tip
Prepare a short decision record highlighting alternatives and expected impacts to speed review.
Key takeaway
Use ARBs for guidance and alignment; keep them advisory and outcome-focused.

screens.title: Running an Effective ARB Review
screens.narratorSegment: Running a productive ARB review requires structure and discipline. Start by time-boxing the meeting and circulating a concise package: goals, key requirements, architecture sketches, and three to five decisions you want feedback on. During the session, the presenter briefly states the problem, the chosen approach, and the main trade-offs. Reviewers then ask focused questions and surface concerns tied to organizational policies or cross-project impact. After discussion, capture specific recommendations and assign owners for follow-up. A short, written outcome—approved, approved with conditions, or revisit—keeps accountability. For example, if the board recommends adding a caching layer for a high-read service, note the expected performance gain and any new failure modes to evaluate. Common misconceptions include treating ARB feedback as optional opinion; instead, log decisions and follow up to ensure boarding leads to measurable action. Keep the board diverse enough to cover security, operations, and design but compact enough to avoid slow schedules. This process reduces ambiguity, ensures consistent standards, and turns review time into a measurable improvement to design quality. What single artifact would you include in every ARB packet to speed decisions?

Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › ARB Review Flow
ARB Review — Step-by-step
A compact process to make reviews efficient and actionable.
1. Pack
Distribute concise artifacts
Goals, constraints, key decisions, and data points.
2. Present
State problems and trade-offs
Focus on three to five specific questions for the board.
3. Discuss
Probing and targeted feedback
Surface operational and cross-project impacts.
4. Record
Capture outcomes

screens.title: Checklists and Questionnaires
screens.narratorSegment: Checklists and questionnaires are low-cost tools for ensuring that common architectural issues are not overlooked. They are predefined sets of actionable questions mapped to best practices or quality attributes. For instance, a security checklist might ask whether external interfaces are authenticated and whether data is encrypted in transit. A resilience checklist might ask whether circuit breakers are used and whether service discovery routes around failed instances. The strength of checklists is speed and repeatability: they provide a consistent baseline that requires minimal training. However, they are inherently limited: they only surface what is asked. They are reactive and cannot detect novel, emergent architectural faults that fall outside listed items. Use checklists as a first pass to catch obvious gaps, and combine them with techniques that explore unknowns, such as prototypes or ARB discussions. In practice, good checklists are categorized by quality attribute and phrased as clear yes/no/N-A questions. That clarity makes them usable in ARB meetings and automated templates. A common pitfall is overly generic items; instead, write specific, actionable items tied to measurable outcomes. Key takeaway: checklists save time and ensure consistency, but do not rely on them alone for complex or novel risks. Which category would you prioritize in your system checklist, and why?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Checklists & Questionnaires
Definition
Actionable, categorized questions

Organize items by quality attribute and make them answerable with Yes/No/N-A to enable rapid evaluation.

Security sample items
  • Are all external interfaces authenticated?
  • Is data encrypted at rest and in transit?
  • Are common web vulnerabilities considered?
Reliability sample items
  • Are circuit breakers in place for remote calls?
  • Is there a failover or retry strategy?
Good practice
Keep items specific and tied to measurable outcomes rather than vague recommendations.
When to use
First pass reviews, ARB pre-checks, or as templates for onboarding teams.
Limitations
They only catch what is listed; novel interactions or subtle trade-offs may be missed.
Example: missing performance interaction
A checklist may verify caching exists but miss that cache invalidation leads to expensive rebuilds under peak load.
Key takeaway
Use checklists for speed and consistency; pair them with targeted experiments for unknown risks.

screens.title: Simulations for Architectural Validation
screens.narratorSegment: Simulations let you reason about performance and scalability without building the entire system. Build a model representing critical components and their interactions, choose realistic workload scenarios, and run experiments to observe metrics like latency, throughput, and queue lengths. For example, a queuing network model can simulate requests flowing through load balancers, service queues, and database connections to predict bottlenecks. Simulations are especially useful when a full implementation is too costly or too late to change. The strength of simulation is the ability to explore 'what-if' scenarios and trade-offs quickly. Their limitation is model fidelity: incorrect assumptions about workloads or resource behavior lead to misleading results. To increase confidence, validate model assumptions against smaller measurements or production traces when available. A common misconception is that simulation results are exact predictions; they are approximations that reveal trends and relative impacts. Use simulation early to narrow architectural options, then confirm with prototypes for the most promising approaches. Key takeaway: simulations expose performance trade-offs with low upfront cost but require careful modeling and validation. What workload assumption would most change your model's outcome? Simulations for Architectural Validation means simulations reveal trends and bottlenecks quickly, but require validated assumptions to be trustworthy.. In practical terms, modeling system behavior under load to predict performance and scalability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Architectural Simulation
What to model
Queues, resources, and workloads

Represent components, service latencies, concurrency limits, and arrival patterns to predict system behavior.

Steps
  1. Define scope and metrics.
  2. Create model of components and interactions.
  3. Run scenarios and analyze trends.
  4. Validate assumptions with small-scale data.
Example
A queuing model predicts that adding worker threads past a threshold yields diminishing latency improvements due to database connection limits.
Strengths
Explore scenarios early with low build cost.
Limitations
Results depend on model fidelity and workload assumptions.
Key takeaway
Use simulations to narrow options, then validate selected designs with prototypes or measurements.

screens.title: Architectural Prototypes
screens.narratorSegment: An architectural prototype is a working, often simplified implementation of a critical component or a vertical slice of the system to validate assumptions. Prototypes are concrete: they exercise real technologies, integration points, and performance characteristics. For example, if a system plans to use a new message queue for inter-service communication, build a prototype that implements the end-to-end path for a representative workload to observe latency, throughput, and error cases. Prototypes are valuable because they produce tangible evidence that a chosen approach will meet requirements. They also uncover integration challenges that design documents and checklists may miss. The downside is development cost and the risk that teams mistake a prototype for production-quality code. Keep prototypes intentionally narrow in scope, time-boxed, and labeled as experiments with clear success criteria. Combine prototypes with ARB discussion and static checks: ARB can suggest what to prototype, and static analysis can later enforce the architecture proven by the prototype. A common misconception is equating a prototype's implementation details with final design; prototypes should inform decisions, not substitute for proper production engineering. Key takeaway: prototypes de-risk high-uncertainty choices through focused, hands-on learning. What integration point would you prototype first?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Prototypes
Definition
Working vertical slices for risky areas

Use prototypes to validate feasibility, performance, and integration of critical components.

Prototype example
Build a message queue integration vertical slice to measure latency and failure behavior under representative load.
Scope guidance
  • Keep scope narrow and time-boxed.
  • Define success criteria up front.
  • Label artifacts as experimental results, not production code.
Benefits
Concrete evidence, early discovery of integration problems, informed decision-making.
Risks
Confusing prototype for final code and underestimating production engineering effort.
Key takeaway
Use prototypes to inform decisions and pair them with governance and automated checks later.

screens.title: Static Analysis for Architectural Compliance
screens.narratorSegment: Static analysis for architectural compliance uses automated tooling to verify that code adheres to predefined architectural rules. This prevents architectural erosion, also known as design drift, by catching violations as code changes. For example, you can configure a rule that prevents the presentation layer from depending directly on the data access layer, ensuring the business logic layer remains the mediator. Tools such as architecture-focused linters are integrated into CI so violations are visible immediately. The primary benefit is continuous enforcement: teams get rapid feedback and correct deviations early. The challenge lies in defining clear, enforceable rules and maintaining them as the architecture evolves. A common misconception is that static rules are too rigid; instead, treat them as guardrails that evolve with deliberate change processes. Practically, start small—enforce a few critical rules—and expand. When a violation occurs, prefer a gradual approach: warn first, then fail builds for repeated or serious infractions. Key takeaway: static analysis preserves intended structure over time and becomes more valuable as codebase size increases. Which core architectural dependency rule would you enforce first in your system? Static Analysis for Architectural Compliance means automated static checks detect forbidden dependencies and maintain structure as code evolves, reducing long-term drift.. In practical terms, automated tools to enforce dependency rules and prevent design drift. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.4 › Static Analysis
What it enforces
Dependency and pattern constraints

Define rules that prevent forbidden interactions and check for adherence during builds.

Practical example (visual)
// Example rule description: Presentation layer must not depend on Data layer.\n// Enforce via tool that scans package dependencies and fails build on violation.
Advantages
Early detection, CI integration, prevents long-term architectural erosion.
Challenges
Rule definition and maintenance, false positives, and evolution with architecture changes.
Suggested rollout
  • Start with a few critical rules.
  • Warn first, then fail builds for repeated violations.
  • Keep rules visible and documented.
Key takeaway
Automated checks are effective guardrails that protect architecture at scale when thoughtfully applied.

screens.title: Strengths and Weaknesses of Each Technique
screens.narratorSegment: Each evaluation technique fills a different role and has trade-offs. ARBs provide cross-project perspective and governance but can slow teams if poorly run. Checklists are fast and cheap, ideal for baseline hygiene, but they cannot find unforeseen interactions. Simulations let you explore performance and scalability trends with low cost, but their usefulness depends on model quality. Prototypes give concrete evidence about feasibility and integration but require development effort and can be mistaken for production-ready code. Static analysis enforces rules continuously and prevents drift but needs clear rules and maintenance. In practice, combine these techniques: use checklists for rapid baseline checks, ARBs for policy alignment, prototypes to de-risk the riskiest components, simulations to explore capacity trade-offs, and static analysis to preserve structure over time. For example, a critical system might undergo an ATAM, be discussed by an ARB for policy, use prototypes for high-risk subsystems, employ simulations for capacity planning, and adopt static rules in CI. The misconception to avoid is picking a single technique and assuming it solves all problems. The key is composition—choose the minimal set that meaningfully reduces your greatest risks. Which combination would you choose for a time-sensitive, safety-critical system?

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we broaden the toolbox for evaluating architectures. You will learn how organizations use standing review groups, lightweight artifacts like checklists, technical experiments such as simulations and prototypes, and automated static checks to validate design choices. These techniques are not a replacement for a rigorous method; they are complementary. An Architecture Review Board leverages collective experience to catch policy and consistency issues early. Checklists and questionnaires provide a quick compliance baseline for common risks like security and scalability. Simulations let you model performance trade-offs without building the whole system. Prototypes provide concrete proofs of feasibility for risky integrations. Static analysis enforces architectural rules continuously, preventing long-term design drift. Choosing among these methods depends on size, criticality, budget, and the quality attributes you must protect. For example, a small team working on an internal tool might rely on checklists and periodic ARB reviews, while a critical system may add prototypes for high-risk components and static rules in CI. As you proceed, think about which mix reduces risk for your project most efficiently. What single risk would you tackle first with the techniques here?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to choose and apply lightweight evaluation techniques that fit your project's constraints. First, you will explore the role, structure, and value of an Architecture Review Board and how it provides consistent oversight across projects. Second, you will learn to design and use checklists and questionnaires to enforce baseline hygiene quickly and consistently. Each objective includes why it matters and a practical example you can use immediately. For instance, you will practice writing checklist questions that explicitly map to a quality attribute like resilience or security, which reduces ambiguity during reviews. You'll also learn when a checklist is insufficient and a deeper prototype or simulation is called for. Finally, you will learn to weigh cost, time, and rigor to select an appropriate mix of techniques. This means balancing advisory reviews, quick checks, hands-on experiments, and automated enforcement to reduce the highest risks with the least delay. Consider a small team with limited budget: these skills help you create a defensible, efficient evaluation plan. Which risk would you eliminate first?

This second objectives slide drills into selection and combination skills. You will learn to compare the strengths and weaknesses of each technique and match them to project context: size, criticality, budget, and available expertise. For example, checklists are inexpensive and fast but miss novel architectural faults; simulations predict performance without full builds but require modeling expertise; prototypes give decisive evidence but cost development time. You will practice a decision flow: identify the highest-risk quality attribute, estimate effort and impact, then choose a minimal evaluation mix that reduces that risk. We will also cover common pitfalls, such as trusting an early prototype as a final design or letting ARBs become slow gatekeepers rather than enablers. By the end, you will be able to propose a tailored evaluation plan — for example, pairing checklists for baseline hygiene, an ARB for policy alignment, a prototype for high-risk components, and static analysis for continuous enforcement. Think about a project you know: which technique would you add first, and why?

An Architecture Review Board is a standing committee of experienced architects and senior technical leaders who review proposed designs and advise teams. The ARB's value is collective experience and organizational consistency: it ensures architectural standards are applied, lessons learned across projects are shared, and potentially risky design decisions are questioned before they propagate. A typical ARB review is structured but less formal than a full ATAM. The presenting architect explains goals, key risks, and major decisions. Reviewers ask probing questions, request clarifications, and may recommend changes or approval. For example, an ARB might flag a proposed direct database access from a presentation component, reminding the team to route through business logic to preserve separation of concerns. A common misconception is that ARBs are gatekeepers who block progress. In healthy practice an ARB is advisory and collaborative: it surfaces constraints and trade-offs, not stop work. To make ARBs effective, define clear scope, keep meetings time-boxed, prepare concise artifacts, and focus on decisions that affect cross-project consistency. Key takeaway: an ARB amplifies organizational wisdom and enforces standards, but it must be structured to enable teams rather than slow them. How would you present a risky decision to an ARB to get constructive guidance?

Running a productive ARB review requires structure and discipline. Start by time-boxing the meeting and circulating a concise package: goals, key requirements, architecture sketches, and three to five decisions you want feedback on. During the session, the presenter briefly states the problem, the chosen approach, and the main trade-offs. Reviewers then ask focused questions and surface concerns tied to organizational policies or cross-project impact. After discussion, capture specific recommendations and assign owners for follow-up. A short, written outcome—approved, approved with conditions, or revisit—keeps accountability. For example, if the board recommends adding a caching layer for a high-read service, note the expected performance gain and any new failure modes to evaluate. Common misconceptions include treating ARB feedback as optional opinion; instead, log decisions and follow up to ensure boarding leads to measurable action. Keep the board diverse enough to cover security, operations, and design but compact enough to avoid slow schedules. This process reduces ambiguity, ensures consistent standards, and turns review time into a measurable improvement to design quality. What single artifact would you include in every ARB packet to speed decisions?

Checklists and questionnaires are low-cost tools for ensuring that common architectural issues are not overlooked. They are predefined sets of actionable questions mapped to best practices or quality attributes. For instance, a security checklist might ask whether external interfaces are authenticated and whether data is encrypted in transit. A resilience checklist might ask whether circuit breakers are used and whether service discovery routes around failed instances. The strength of checklists is speed and repeatability: they provide a consistent baseline that requires minimal training. However, they are inherently limited: they only surface what is asked. They are reactive and cannot detect novel, emergent architectural faults that fall outside listed items. Use checklists as a first pass to catch obvious gaps, and combine them with techniques that explore unknowns, such as prototypes or ARB discussions. In practice, good checklists are categorized by quality attribute and phrased as clear yes/no/N-A questions. That clarity makes them usable in ARB meetings and automated templates. A common pitfall is overly generic items; instead, write specific, actionable items tied to measurable outcomes. Key takeaway: checklists save time and ensure consistency, but do not rely on them alone for complex or novel risks. Which category would you prioritize in your system checklist, and why?

Simulations let you reason about performance and scalability without building the entire system. Build a model representing critical components and their interactions, choose realistic workload scenarios, and run experiments to observe metrics like latency, throughput, and queue lengths. For example, a queuing network model can simulate requests flowing through load balancers, service queues, and database connections to predict bottlenecks. Simulations are especially useful when a full implementation is too costly or too late to change. The strength of simulation is the ability to explore 'what-if' scenarios and trade-offs quickly. Their limitation is model fidelity: incorrect assumptions about workloads or resource behavior lead to misleading results. To increase confidence, validate model assumptions against smaller measurements or production traces when available. A common misconception is that simulation results are exact predictions; they are approximations that reveal trends and relative impacts. Use simulation early to narrow architectural options, then confirm with prototypes for the most promising approaches. Key takeaway: simulations expose performance trade-offs with low upfront cost but require careful modeling and validation. What workload assumption would most change your model's outcome? Simulations for Architectural Validation means simulations reveal trends and bottlenecks quickly, but require validated assumptions to be trustworthy.. In practical terms, modeling system behavior under load to predict performance and scalability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An architectural prototype is a working, often simplified implementation of a critical component or a vertical slice of the system to validate assumptions. Prototypes are concrete: they exercise real technologies, integration points, and performance characteristics. For example, if a system plans to use a new message queue for inter-service communication, build a prototype that implements the end-to-end path for a representative workload to observe latency, throughput, and error cases. Prototypes are valuable because they produce tangible evidence that a chosen approach will meet requirements. They also uncover integration challenges that design documents and checklists may miss. The downside is development cost and the risk that teams mistake a prototype for production-quality code. Keep prototypes intentionally narrow in scope, time-boxed, and labeled as experiments with clear success criteria. Combine prototypes with ARB discussion and static checks: ARB can suggest what to prototype, and static analysis can later enforce the architecture proven by the prototype. A common misconception is equating a prototype's implementation details with final design; prototypes should inform decisions, not substitute for proper production engineering. Key takeaway: prototypes de-risk high-uncertainty choices through focused, hands-on learning. What integration point would you prototype first?

Static analysis for architectural compliance uses automated tooling to verify that code adheres to predefined architectural rules. This prevents architectural erosion, also known as design drift, by catching violations as code changes. For example, you can configure a rule that prevents the presentation layer from depending directly on the data access layer, ensuring the business logic layer remains the mediator. Tools such as architecture-focused linters are integrated into CI so violations are visible immediately. The primary benefit is continuous enforcement: teams get rapid feedback and correct deviations early. The challenge lies in defining clear, enforceable rules and maintaining them as the architecture evolves. A common misconception is that static rules are too rigid; instead, treat them as guardrails that evolve with deliberate change processes. Practically, start small—enforce a few critical rules—and expand. When a violation occurs, prefer a gradual approach: warn first, then fail builds for repeated or serious infractions. Key takeaway: static analysis preserves intended structure over time and becomes more valuable as codebase size increases. Which core architectural dependency rule would you enforce first in your system? Static Analysis for Architectural Compliance means automated static checks detect forbidden dependencies and maintain structure as code evolves, reducing long-term drift.. In practical terms, automated tools to enforce dependency rules and prevent design drift. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Each evaluation technique fills a different role and has trade-offs. ARBs provide cross-project perspective and governance but can slow teams if poorly run. Checklists are fast and cheap, ideal for baseline hygiene, but they cannot find unforeseen interactions. Simulations let you explore performance and scalability trends with low cost, but their usefulness depends on model quality. Prototypes give concrete evidence about feasibility and integration but require development effort and can be mistaken for production-ready code. Static analysis enforces rules continuously and prevents drift but needs clear rules and maintenance. In practice, combine these techniques: use checklists for rapid baseline checks, ARBs for policy alignment, prototypes to de-risk the riskiest components, simulations to explore capacity trade-offs, and static analysis to preserve structure over time. For example, a critical system might undergo an ATAM, be discussed by an ARB for policy, use prototypes for high-risk subsystems, employ simulations for capacity planning, and adopt static rules in CI. The misconception to avoid is picking a single technique and assuming it solves all problems. The key is composition—choose the minimal set that meaningfully reduces your greatest risks. Which combination would you choose for a time-sensitive, safety-critical system?
